Dermatology · published research

Contact dermatitis

Two animal studies report reduced inflammation in selected allergic contact dermatitis models, while irritant dermatitis was not improved. No human treatment study was identified.

PBM Database summary

What the records report

Two animal studies report reduced inflammation in selected allergic contact dermatitis models, while irritant dermatitis was not improved. No human treatment study was identified.

Summary of the Evidence

Two publications examine contact dermatitis in separate mouse experiments. Each includes mechanistic assays within the same paper, not additional studies. One tested isolated naïve T cells and the other ex-vivo rat mast cells. No human clinical study was identified.

Human and clinical evidence

No study has tested PBM in people with allergic or irritant contact dermatitis. Findings concern experimental inflammation rather than patient symptoms or recurrence.

Animal evidence

Fu et al. reported reduced skin inflammation and fewer T cells after PBM in a mouse allergic contact dermatitis model (2024).

In an earlier mouse-ear experiment, helium-neon treatment reduced allergic dermatitis swelling but not irritant dermatitis swelling. Treatment five minutes after challenge increased the swelling measure (Sakihama 1995).

In-vitro and ex-vivo evidence

Fu et al. found moderated naïve T-cell activation with results implicating TGF-beta signaling. Sakihama’s rat mast-cell assay found lower spontaneous histamine release, but not release induced by substance P or compound 48/80. These assays are components of the two papers, not separate replications.

Treatment Parameters and Generalizability

The 1995 study used 632.8-nm helium-neon light, red visible light, at 12.2 J/cm² and tested several timings around the challenge. Parameter detail in the newer paper is insufficient for comparison. No human dose-finding study establishes a schedule.

Interpretation

Results support a narrow effect in selected allergic models, not contact dermatitis generally. Human benefit remains untested, while the irritant-model and timing results limit broad conclusions.

Evidence strength in source summaryVery low for changes in experimental allergic contact dermatitis
Publications and records2 articles

Evidence strength rationale and next steps

Both direct papers are controlled experiments, but they use animal models and linked laboratory assays rather than patient treatment. The older results differ between allergic and irritant dermatitis, and the direction also depends on when light is given. Independent replication with standardized timing, followed by a controlled study in people with a defined dermatitis subtype, would support a stronger rating.
